strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant and well-motivated problem setting: safe RL where both the cost function and the safety budget are unknown, and feedback is only available as sparse, trajectory-level binary safety labels. This is a weaker and more realistic feedback model than most prior work (ICRL requires expert demonstrations; RLSF requires a known budget), and the positioning against these lines of work is clear.

The core idea of factorizing the trajectory-level safety probability into per-timestep multiplicative scores (SSV model) is a clean and intuitive formulation of safety credit assignment from sparse labels, and the recurrent summary-vector architecture that supports using the scores as an augmented state for PPO-Lagrangian is sensible and scalable.

The empirical evaluation is fairly broad: 12 continuous-control tasks across Safety Gymnasium, MuJoCo velocity tasks, and Bullet Safety Gym, with 8 seeds, an oracle PPO-Lagrangian baseline, and the closest prior method (RLSF). The SSV model produces safe policies on all tasks with returns close to the oracle, whereas the C&B baseline fails on several tasks, and SSV uses fewer labeled trajectories than RLSF in several domains.

The paper goes beyond final performance and includes diagnostic analyses of the learned credit assignment (Figures 2-4, 8-13), showing that inferred cost concentrates around the critical timestep where cumulative cost crosses the budget, and the selective-feedback (CV-based) strategy is ablated against labeling all trajectories (Table 3).

The proposed constraint reformulation (fraction of safe trajectories >= d) is honestly framed as an approximation, and the direction of the Jensen's inequality relaxation (constraining the lower bound implies the original constraint) is used correctly.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is thin and partly overstated. Proposition 3.3 is a trivial telescoping identity presented as a proposition with a proof; P̂Δt = P̂(ψ0:t)/P̂(ψ0:t-1) is a ratio of marginal probabilities of prefixes, not a genuinely causal per-step credit, and the interpretation as the cost incurred at step t is only heuristic. The formal statements (Lemma 3.4, Corollary 3.5) are informal and rely on an unquantified MLE consistency argument that ignores the substantial distribution shift between the offline pretraining data and the evolving policy during online RL.

There is a substantive soundness gap in the reformulation. The discounting step from equation 9 to 10 (applying gamma to the sum of log P̂Δt) breaks the connection to the constraint being derived: the discounted sum being >= log d does not preserve the original (undiscounted) product constraint, and no corrected threshold or justification is given. Moreover, the reformulated constraint E[Ψ(τ)] >= d is a different problem than the original budget constraint E[Σ γ^t C] <= b in equation 1, but the paper does not formally relate the two; comparisons to the oracle PPO-Lagrangian on the budget constraint are therefore somewhat apples-to-oranges and the near-oracle reward results may partly reflect the looser percentile-style constraint.

Assumption 3.6 (monotonically non-increasing prefix safety probabilities) is asserted to hold by construction, but it is not enforced in the training objective (standard BCE loss), and nothing in the experiments verifies whether the learned model satisfies it; the model could assign P̂Δt > 1 or violate monotonicity on out-of-distribution trajectories.

Baseline coverage is limited. There is no comparison to any inverse constrained RL or constraint-inference baseline (e.g., Malik et al. 2021, Liu et al. 2023), even though the paper motivates the setting against ICRL; the empirical claims rest on one learned-cost competitor (RLSF) plus an oracle. RLSF also achieves comparable or better cost-reward tradeoffs on several Safety Gymnasium tasks (e.g., PointCircle1/2), which the text does not fully acknowledge.

Several experimental details needed for reproducibility are missing or vague: no code release is mentioned, hyperparameters for the SSV model and Lagrangian tuning are not reported in the main text, how gradient information flows from the safety model into the cost critic during RL is underspecified, and the '95% accuracy' pretraining criterion and its sensitivity are not analyzed. The DSRL offline dataset used for pretraining is a notable additional data requirement that is not ablated (e.g., performance vs. pretraining data quantity/coverage).

Presentation has notable defects: typos ('trainng', 'Modification are required', 'difficulty to specify'), Figure 1 is difficult to parse, the C&B model description is deferred entirely to the appendix, and there is no explicit limitations section despite several important caveats (distribution shift, sensitivity to feedback quality/label noise, inability to handle non-monotone safety) that a careful discussion should cover.

Some reported results undermine the 'safe across all tasks' narrative at the margins: several SSV cost values sit at or near the budget of 25 (e.g., Walker2d 24.1 (3.9), BallRun 24.7 (0.8), CarRun 23.3 (1.1)), and Table 3 shows the DroneRun cost degrading to 32.0 (45.6) when all trajectories are labeled, suggesting some fragility across seeds that is not discussed.

strengths: The problem setting is well-motivated and practically relevant: learning both the cost function AND the budget from sparsely (trajectory-level) labeled data is a strictly weaker supervision assumption than prior work such as RLSF (known budget) and ICRL (expert demonstrations), and the paper clearly positions itself against these baselines.

The empirical evaluation is reasonably broad: 12 continuous control tasks across Safety Gymnasium, MuJoCo, and Bullet Safety Gym, 8 seeds, an oracle PPO-Lagrangian baseline and the RLSF baseline, with the SSV-based method achieving safe policies across all tasks with reward close to the oracle.

The safety summary vector (SSV) architecture, which maintains a compact summary vector h_t so that log P_hat_t^Delta is a function of (s_t, a_t, h_t), is a sensible design that makes the learned safety signal usable inside model-free PPO-Lagrangian without breaking Markovianity.

The credit assignment analysis (Figures 2-4, 8-13) goes beyond raw RL metrics and provides qualitative evidence that the inferred per-timestep safety signal concentrates near the critical timesteps where the true budget is crossed and is low in cost-free 'flat regions'.
The paper is honest that the C&B baseline struggles on several tasks and includes an ablation (Table 3) of the selective-feedback (CV-based) trajectory selection strategy.
weaknesses: The central theoretical result (Proposition 3.3) is a trivial telescoping identity: equation (3) is a tautological product of ratios that cancels by construction. Presenting this as the key contribution of 'credit assignment' oversells what is essentially algebraic re-parameterization of prefix probabilities, not a learned credit assignment mechanism with guarantees.

The 'proof' of Lemma 3.4 is not sound as stated. It appeals to MLE consistency 'as training sample size tends to infinity' to claim E[Psi(tau)] approximately E[P_hat(psi=1|tau)], but this ignores (a) model misspecification, and (b) distribution shift: the constraint model is trained on buffered/dataset trajectories, yet the expectation is taken under pi_theta, which changes continuously during safe RL. The approximation argument does not cover the regime in which the method is actually used.

The move from equation (9) to equation (10) is unprincipled: applying the reward discount gamma^t to the sum of log safety scores changes the constraint semantics. The labeling function Psi is defined on undiscounted total cost (Section 2.2), so a discounted log-safety constraint does not approximate constraint (7); it systematically weakens the constraint as horizon grows, and the paper provides no analysis of when this approximation is valid.

The credit assignment is empirically delayed: the authors themselves report that 'the inferred cost signal is typically highest in the next five timesteps immediately following the critical timestep.' For a safety-critical method, delayed attribution of several steps is a material limitation that is acknowledged only in passing and not analyzed for its effect on constraint satisfaction.

Statistical rigor is limited: results are reported as mean (std) over 8 seeds but no significance tests or confidence statements are given, and many cost comparisons (e.g., PointCircle1: PPO-Lagrangian 21.5 vs SSV 16.2 with stds of ~7) are within noise. Several 'safe' designations are based on visually comparing noisy means to the budget of 25.

The labeled-trajectory comparison is apples-to-oranges: SSV uses the CV-based selective feedback while C&B is given a fixed 6000-12000 labeled trajectories 'since the selective feedback of section C.2 is not easily applicable' -- so the claim of 'requiring fewer labeled trajectories than RLSF in several domains' conflates method and feedback-schedule differences.

Presentation errors undermine confidence: the experiment setup states 'trajectory is only labeled safe if the true cost incurred is above the threshold', which inverts the labeling function defined in Section 2.2; there are multiple typos ('trainng', 'difficulty to specify'); the C&B baseline (used for half the comparisons) is relegated to an appendix with minimal detail; and Jensen's inequality in equation (9) is presented as if it solves the estimation problem when it only produces a (conservative) bound.

Assumption 3.6 (prefix safety probabilities monotonically non-increasing) is asserted to be non-restrictive, but nothing in the architecture enforces it, and no empirical check of its violation frequency is provided.

Reproducibility concerns: no code release is mentioned; key hyperparameters of the constraint models (SSV network size, retraining schedule, CV thresholds) and of the pre-training on DSRL are not specified in the manuscript.

Practicality of the feedback model is under-examined: during online training a script implementing the true labeling function labels variable-length trajectory segments on demand. The paper does not discuss how a human annotator would label arbitrary-length trajectory segments in real deployments, which is the very motivation for the sparse-feedback setting.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant and well-motivated setting: safe RL when both the cost function and budget are unknown, and only trajectory-level binary safety labels (weaker supervision than state-level feedback or expert demonstrations required by ICRL) are available. This fills a genuine gap relative to ICRL and human-feedback-based constraint learning.

The proposed Safety Summary Vector (SSV) model is a reasonable architectural solution: decomposing trajectory safety probability into per-timestep multiplicative factors and using a summary vector h_t as an augmented state makes the learned constraint compatible with model-free CRL methods such as PPO-Lagrangian.

The empirical evaluation is reasonably thorough: 12 continuous control tasks across three benchmark suites (Safety Gymnasium, MuJoCo velocity, Bullet Safety Gym), 8 seeds, evaluation on 100 held-out test trajectories in a separate environment, and comparisons against the oracle PPO-Lagrangian and the closest prior method RLSF. The main result—that SSV+TraCeS yields safe policies across all twelve tasks with return close to the oracle, while the C&B baseline fails on several tasks—is a meaningful finding.

The credit-assignment analysis (Figures 2–4, 8–13) goes beyond end-task metrics and provides evidence that the learned per-timestep scores concentrate around the critical timestep when cumulative cost crosses the budget and stay low in 'flat' cost regions, supporting the central interpretability claim.

The selective feedback strategy (CV-based trajectory selection, Appendix C.2) is a sensible addition, and the ablation (Table 3) honestly reports that it reduces labeled trajectories (2,627–6,521 vs. fixed 6,000/12,000 for baselines) with comparable performance.
weaknesses: The theoretical development is thinner than the framing suggests. Proposition 3.3 is essentially a telescoping identity—the per-timestep scores are defined as ratios of consecutive sub-trajectory probability estimates, so the 'decomposition' is true by construction rather than a structural result about learning. Lemma 3.4 relies on a consistency argument ('as training sample size tends to infinity') with no finite-sample or distribution-shift analysis, which matters here because the model is continually retrained on an evolving policy distribution.

The problem reformulation changes the safety semantics in ways that are not fully acknowledged. The original CMDP constraint E[Σ γ^t C(s_t,a_t)] ≤ b is replaced by E[Ψ(τ)] ≥ d (proportion of safe trajectories ≥ 0.9), which is a chance-constraint-like surrogate, not equivalent to the original expected-cost constraint. Satisfying the surrogate does not in general imply satisfying the original constraint, and the paper does not formally connect d to the unknown b. This should be stated as a limitation of the guarantees.

The application of the discount rate to the sum of log P̂Δ_t in Equation 10 is explicitly motivated as a computational convenience ('to make the sum finite') rather than a principled choice; discounting log-probabilities alters the constraint's meaning, and the interaction between γ, T, and log d is not analyzed.

Assumption 3.6 (monotonically non-increasing safety probability) is a property of the true labeling function, but the learned model P̂ can violate it during training; how violations affect the PPO-Lagrangian optimization and constraint satisfaction is not discussed.

Some empirical results raise questions about robustness: evaluated costs for SSV sometimes sit near or slightly above the budget (e.g., Walker2d 24.1 (3.9) with budget 25; BallRun 24.7 (0.8)), and the 'All feedback' variant of SSV fails on DroneRun (cost 32.0 (45.6)), while PPO-Lagrangian itself shows large cost violations in evaluation (e.g., Hopper 29.1 (36.2)), suggesting evaluation-cost variance issues that deserve more analysis. No statistical significance tests are reported.

The setup partially undermines the 'unknown constraint' claim: sparse labels are generated by a script implementing the true labeling function over a curated offline dataset (DSRL), and models are pre-trained to 95% accuracy. This is a reasonable experimental proxy, but it assumes access to a reasonably diverse labeled dataset whose coverage of the constraint is never stress-tested (e.g., sensitivity to label budget, dataset bias, or distribution shift is not studied).

Reproducibility is incomplete: no code release is mentioned, and key hyperparameters (network sizes for the SSV encoder/decoder, Lagrange multiplier update rates, retraining schedule, thresholds for the CV selection) are not provided even in the appendix.

Presentation needs polish: several typos and grammatical errors ('trainng', 'Modification are required', 'It can be observed from the figure that the inferred cost typically peaks when the accumulated cost reaches 25'), and the C&B model details are deferred to the appendix, making Section 3.1 hard to assess in the main text.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: safe RL from sparse binary trajectory/prefix accept-reject labels under a monotone (irreversible) violation abstraction, where neither the cost function nor the threshold is known. This zero-knowledge setting is well distinguished from oracle CMDP solvers and from partial-knowledge prior work (RLSF).

The core technical idea is clean and sensible: factorizing the trajectory-level non-violation probability into per-step multiplicative credits (Prop. 4.2), which yields a dense per-step surrogate cost and enables plugging into standard CMDP machinery (PPO-Lagrangian). The Jensen-gap analysis (Theorem 4.5 / A.1) is correct and the paper is appropriately honest that it is a worst-case diagnostic bound rather than a tight certificate.

Empirically thorough evaluation: 12 tasks across three benchmark suites, 8 random seeds, comparisons against oracle ceilings (PPO-Lagrangian, CPPO-PID, CUP, FOCOPS, TRPO-Saute), a partial-knowledge method (RLSF), and a zero-knowledge baseline, with a matched-label-budget comparison (Table 6).

Extensive and well-designed ablations: low-data regime (1000 labels), random initialization without offline pretraining, CV vs. random trajectory selection, sensitivity to the acceptability rate d, label noise up to 20%, log-credit clamping, checkpoint sparsity, terminal-only labels, and an alternative threshold b=50. These support the robustness claims rather than just cherry-picking settings.

Qualitative analysis goes beyond aggregate metrics: trajectory-level score calibration (Fig. 3), per-timestep attribution near the violation event (Fig. 4, 6), and attribution ratios in true zero-cost regions (Fig. 5) provide evidence that the learned credits are localized rather than uniform.
A small human feedback study (Appendix C.9) with blind annotation adds external validity beyond simulator-constructed labels, and the paper honestly frames it as limited in scale.

Good reproducibility: code is released, hyperparameters are fully specified (Table 2), the pseudocode is given, computational overhead is reported (+4-4.4% vs. PPO-Lagrangian), and the offline pretraining data source is disclosed.
Honest limitations discussion (Appendix E) covering training-time violations, dependence on a labeling pipeline, and non-stationary/inconsistent supervision.
weaknesses: The theory is relatively light: Lemma 4.4 relies on realizability and 'small optimization/generalization error' assumptions that are not quantified, and the Jensen-gap bound is loose for long horizons (the paper itself acknowledges p_hat >= exp(-7T)). The guarantees are thus largely diagnostic, and the central claim of safe behavior rests on the empirical results rather than theory.

The zero-knowledge baseline landscape is thin: the only direct zero-knowledge competitor (C-T) is a baseline designed by the authors themselves. Adapting a preference-based/constraint-learning method to this setting, or comparing against other feedback-based cost-learning approaches, would strengthen the claim that TraCeS's factorization (rather than just any learned signal) is what drives the gains.

Constraint satisfaction is marginal on several tasks (e.g., Walker2d cost 24.1 vs. threshold 25; HalfCheetah 22.4) with substantial variance across seeds, and no statistical significance testing is reported for the aggregate comparisons. Evaluation uses 100 trajectories per policy, which is reasonable but leaves the near-boundary results statistically fragile.

The warm-start pretraining from an offline safe RL dataset (Liu et al., 2024) means the main results are not purely online label-free learning; the random-initialization ablation (C.7) covers only 4 of 12 tasks, so the dependence on pretraining across the full suite is not fully established.

The monotone/irreversible violation assumption restricts applicability; for the motivating autonomous-driving example (temporary lane deviation), violations are arguably reversible. The paper motivates the work partly with this example but then narrows to irreversible violations, and the gap between the motivating setting and the formal setting is not fully closed.

The surrogate cost is stochastic (sampled from a log-normal per step) and clamped; while the clamp sensitivity study mitigates concerns, the interaction between sampling noise, the recurrent summary state h_t, and non-Markovian conditioning of the policy/critics could use deeper analysis.
The human study is small (3 seeds, 10 evaluation rollouts per seed, one task, reward learning disabled), so its evidence value is limited even though it is honestly presented.

strengths: The problem setting — safe RL when both the cost function and threshold are unknown and supervision is limited to coarse accept/reject labels — is practically relevant and clearly motivated (Section 1, Appendix B.1).

The core idea of factorizing a trajectory-level non-violation probability into per-step multiplicative credits (Proposition 4.2) is a clean, interpretable decomposition that yields a dense per-step surrogate cost compatible with standard CMDP solvers.

The empirical evaluation is broad: 12 tasks across three benchmark suites, 8 seeds, ablations on trajectory selection, label noise, checkpoint sparsity, clamping, the acceptability-rate parameter d, an alternative threshold (b=50), and a small human annotation study.

The writing is generally clear, and the paper is candid in places (e.g., acknowledging the Jensen-gap bound is loose, that learned credits are surrogates rather than identifiable recovery of hidden costs, and a limitations appendix).
weaknesses: The central 'sparse trajectory-level labels' claim is overstated relative to the actual experimental setup. The main experiments use prefix/segment labels every 5 timesteps on Run tasks and every 20 timesteps on MuJoCo/Circle tasks (Appendix B.4.1) — i.e., 20–40+ labels per trajectory, which is semi-dense supervision. When supervision is genuinely sparse (terminal-only labels, Appendix C.14), performance degrades substantially and the policy violates the constraint on HalfCheetah (cost 50.8 vs. threshold 25) and marginally on AntRun (26.6), undercutting the headline claim.

The theoretical contribution is thin. Proposition 4.2 is a trivial telescoping identity; Theorem 4.5 is a generic second-order Taylor bound on the log function, and with the clamping-induced floor p̂_τ ≥ exp(-7T), the bound 1/(2ε²)·Var (and the worst-case (1-ε)²/(8ε²)) is vacuous for long horizons — which the authors themselves concede. Lemma 4.4 is essentially an assumption ('if p̂_τ is a good proxy...') dressed as a result, with no analysis of the distribution-shift or non-stationarity introduced by iteratively retraining the estimator on the current policy's own rollouts.

The 'zero-knowledge' framing is weakened by undisclosed-seeming dependencies: both TraCeS and RLSF are pretrained on an offline safe RL dataset (Appendix B.4.1), and label construction relies on oracle costs. The estimated cost is history-dependent (a function of h_t), so the resulting problem is not Markov; conditioning the actor and constraint critic on h_t is a heuristic patch whose interaction with the estimator's own non-stationarity is not analyzed.

Constraint satisfaction is marginal on many tasks: TraCeS costs sit at or near the threshold of 25 on Walker2d (24.1 ± 3.9), HalfCheetah (22.4), BallRun (24.7 ± 0.8), CarRun (23.3 ± 1.1), and AntRun (21.4), so 'reliably learns constraint-satisfying policies' is not well supported — several seeds likely violate, and bolding based on means obscures this. Rewards are also frequently below both oracle solvers and sometimes below the C-T baseline (e.g., Ant, Walker2d, AntRun).

The only like-for-like zero-knowledge baseline is a simple MLP (C-T) designed by the authors; the sole external baseline (RLSF) is partial-knowledge and unsupported on a third of the suite, making the empirical comparison base thin.

The human study is very small (one task, 100 labeled trajectories per seed, 3 seeds, 10 evaluation rollouts per method, a single annotator), limiting the claimed evidence of robustness to real human feedback.
The code link in the paper is incomplete (footnote 1 truncates at 'https://github.com/'), which harms reproducibility despite otherwise detailed hyperparameter reporting.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly formulated problem: learning per-timestep violation credit from sparse binary trajectory/prefix labels when neither the cost function nor the threshold is known, which is a real gap relative to standard CMDP methods and prior feedback-based approaches (e.g., RLSF assumes a known threshold).

The multiplicative (survival-style) factorization of non-violation probability into per-step credits is an elegant and interpretable design, with a clean Jensen-gap analysis (Theorem 4.5) that is honestly characterized as a loose, worst-case diagnostic bound rather than oversold as a tight certificate.

Empirically comprehensive: 12 tasks across three benchmark suites, 8 seeds, baselines grouped by knowledge level (oracle / partial / zero-knowledge), plus extensive ablations (low-data regime, label noise, trajectory-selection strategy, clamp sensitivity, checkpoint sparsity, terminal-only labels, alternative threshold b=50, random initialization without pretraining, and a small human feedback study).

Strong honesty throughout: limitations are explicitly discussed (Appendix E), the identifiability weakness of the C-T baseline is acknowledged, the looseness of the theoretical bound is admitted, and the learned credits are carefully positioned as 'control-relevant surrogates' rather than recoverable ground-truth costs.
Qualitative analysis (Figures 3-6) goes beyond aggregate metrics to verify calibration and localized credit assignment, which directly supports the central credit-assignment claim.

Concrete reproducibility support: code release, hyperparameter tables, computational overhead measurements, and detailed implementation notes (e.g., conditioning policy/critic on the estimator summary h_t).
weaknesses: Gap between the advertised supervision sparsity and the experimental setup: the headline claim is learning from 'sparse trajectory-level labels,' but the main experiments use prefix/segment labels every 20 timesteps (MuJoCo/Circle) and every 5 timesteps (Run tasks). Labels every 5 steps are nearly dense, so the primary results do not fully exercise the claimed setting; the terminal-only experiment (C.14) shows clear degradation, meaning the strongest version of the claim is not the one demonstrated in Table 1.

The theory defers the crucial assumption: Lemma 4.4 assumes p̂_τ 'is a good proxy' for the acceptability indicator, which is precisely the hard part of the problem. The Jensen-gap bound (a straightforward Taylor/Pinch-remainder argument) bounds only the relaxation error, not the safety of the resulting policy under estimator error or distribution shift; no guarantee connects surrogate constraint satisfaction to true constraint satisfaction.

The main zero-knowledge baseline (C-T) is a simple self-designed MLP with acknowledged identifiability pathologies; there are no external zero-knowledge baselines, so the 'substantially more label-efficient than zero-knowledge baselines' claim rests on a comparison against a weak, self-built reference.
The matched-label-budget comparison with RLSF (C.3) covers only three of twelve tasks, so the label-efficiency claim against the strongest partial-knowledge baseline is only partially substantiated.

The human feedback study is very small (one task, 3 seeds, 100 labels, 10 evaluation rollouts per seed) and disables reward learning; its evidential value is limited even though the authors flag this.

Conditioning the policy on the recurrent summary h_t makes the learned policy history-dependent, which slightly confounds comparison against Markov CMDP baselines and complicates interpretation of the CMDP reformulation.

Some main-table results sit close to or overlap the violation boundary (e.g., Walker2d cost 24.1±3.9 vs. threshold 25; AntRun 21.4±1.9), so constraint satisfaction on the hardest tasks is less decisive than the summary text suggests.
